questions.q: A force $\mathrm{F}=\alpha+\beta \mathrm{x}^2$ acts on an object in the x -direction. The work done by the force is 5 J when the object is displaced by 1 m . If the constant $\alpha=1 \mathrm{~N}$ then $\beta$ will be
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$F=\alpha+\beta x^2$
Work done $\int d w=\int F \cdot d x\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \Delta W=\int F \cdot d x=\int\left(\alpha+\beta x^2\right) d x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \Delta W=\left|\alpha x+\frac{\beta x^3}{3}\right|_0^1=\alpha+\frac{\beta}{3}=5
\end{aligned}$
Given $\alpha=1$
So, $\frac{\beta}{3}=4\Rightarrow \beta=12 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$

questions.q: A bob of mass m is suspended by a light string of length L. It is imparted a minimum horizontal velocity at the lowest point A such that it just completes half circle reaching the top most position B. The ratio of kinetic energies ( K.E. )A( K.E. )B is :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The velocity given is minimum, just enough to complete verticle circle. At the top most point, tension of the string will be zero and gravitational force will provide the required centripetal force.

Therefore, 

mg=mVH2L⇒12mVH2=12gL

Apply energy conservation between point A and B, we get

12mVL2=12mVH2+mg(2 L)

⇒VL=5gL

Also, VH=gL

Required ratio, (K.E)A(K.E)B=12 m(5gL)212 m(gL)2=51

questions.q: A particle of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>m</mi></math> is moving in a circular path of constant radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> such that its centripetal acceleration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></math> is varying with time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi></math> as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>r</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> , where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math> is a constant. The power delivered to the particle by the force acting on it is -
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
ac=k2rt2

Or v2r=k2rt2  Or  v=krt
Therefore, tangential acceleration, at=dvdt=kr

Therefore, tangential force, Ft=mat=mkr

Only tangential force does work.

Power=Ftv=mkrkrt ⇒Power=mk2r2t

questions.q: An object of mass 1000 g experiences a time dependent force $\vec{F}=\left(2 t \hat{i}+3 t^2 \hat{j}\right) N$. The power generated by the force at time $t$ is :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=(2 t \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \mathrm{t} \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{N} \\ & \mathrm{m}=1000 \mathrm{gm}=1 \mathrm{~kg} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~F}}=m \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=2 \mathrm{t} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \mathrm{t}^2 \hat{j} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=2 t \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \mathrm{t}^2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}\end{aligned}$
$\vec{v}=t^2 \hat{i}+t^3 \hat{j}$
Power, $\mathrm{P}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}$
$\begin{aligned} & P=\left(2 t \hat{i}+3 t^2 \hat{j}\right) \cdot\left(t^2 \hat{i}+t^3 \hat{j}\right) \\ & P=\left(2 t^3+3 t^5\right) W\end{aligned}$

The work done by the net force during its displacement from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> is  (Take <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>25</mn><mo> </mo><msup><mrow><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>).
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, work done by all forces will be is equal to the change in kinetic energy.

Wall=ΔK

=12mb2x25-x15 =12×0.5×116×45=16 J

questions.q:
Water falls from a 40 m high dam at the rate of 9×104 kg per hour. Fifty percentage of gravitational potential energy can be converted into electrical energy. Using this hydro electric energy number of 100 W lamps, that can be lit, is

questions.solution:
Since 50% efficiency is given, half of the energy of the falling water will be used by the bulbs. Therefore,

12∆mghΔt=n×P⇒12×9×1043600×10×40=100n⇒n=50

Applying conservation of mechanical energy between point A & B, we get

KEA+UA=KEB+UB

⇒0+mg(1)=12mv2+mg×0.5

⇒v=g=10 m s-1

questions.q: A body of mass 4 kg is placed on a plane at a point P having coordinate $(3,4) \mathrm{m}$. Under the action of force $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) \mathrm{N}$, it moves to a new point Q having coordinates $(6,10) \mathrm{m}$ in 4 sec . The average power and instanteous power at the end of 4 sec are in the ratio of :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \langle\mathrm{p}\rangle=\frac{(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \cdot(3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+6 \hat{\mathrm{j}})}{4}=6 \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}}{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{2} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\frac{3}{4} \hat{\mathrm{j}}\right) \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \text { at } \mathrm{t}=4 \mathrm{sec}=\left(\frac{1}{2} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\frac{3}{4} \hat{\mathrm{j}}\right) \times 4=(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \\ & P_{\text {ins }}=(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3)(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}})=13 \\ & \frac{\langle\mathrm{P}\rangle}{P_{\text {ins }}}=\frac{6}{13}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ moves on a straight line with its velocity increasing with distance according to the equation $v=\alpha \sqrt{x}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant. The total work done by all the forces applied on the particle during its displacement from $x=0$ to $x=\mathrm{d}$, will be :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{v}=\alpha \sqrt{\mathrm{x}} \\ & \text { at } \mathrm{x}=0: \mathrm{v}=0 \\ & \& \text { at } \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{d} ; \mathrm{v}=\alpha \sqrt{\mathrm{d}} \\ & \text { W.D }=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}} \\ & \text { W.D }=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(\alpha \sqrt{\mathrm{d}})^2-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}(0)^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \text { W.D }=\frac{\mathrm{m} \alpha^2 \mathrm{~d}}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A particle is released from height $S$ above the surface of the earth. At certain height its kinetic energy is three times its potential energy. The height from the surface of the earth and the speed of the particle at that instant are respectively.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{V}^2=0+2 \mathrm{~g}(\mathrm{~S}-\mathrm{x}) \\ & \mathrm{V}^2=2 \mathrm{~g}(\mathrm{~S}-\mathrm{x})
\end{aligned}$
At B, Potential energy $=m g x$
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{mgx}=3 \times \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2 \\ & \mathrm{gx}=\frac{3}{2} \times 2 \mathrm{~g}(\mathrm{~S}-\mathrm{x}) \\ & 4 \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{S} \\ & \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{S}}{4}
\end{aligned}$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{V}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \times \frac{3 \mathrm{~S}}{4}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{gS}}{2}}$

questions.q: As per the given figure, two blocks each of mass 250 g are connected to a spring of spring constant 2 N m-1. If both are given velocity v in opposite directions, then maximum elongation of the spring is
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let the maximum elongation of the spring be x.

Using energy conservation

Loss in kinetic energy of both blocks=Gain in spring energy

12mv2×2=12kx2

⇒0.25v2=12×2×x2

⇒14v2=12×2×x2

∴x=v2

questions.q: A force acts on a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi> </mi><mi>kg</mi></math> object so that its position is given as a function of time as <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo></math> What is the work done by this force in first <math><mn>5</mn></math> seconds?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Here, the position of the object is x=3t2+5, therefore the velocity of the object will be,

v=dxdt=d3t2+5dt

v=6t+0

From the work-energy theorem, all the work done by the force acting on it will be equal to the change in its kinetic energy, i.e.,

W=KEt=5 s-KEt=0 s
W=12×2×6×52-12×2×6×02
W=900 J.

v2=2v1

P=mv

P2=mv2=2mv1

P1=mv1

% change =ΔPP1×100=2mv1-mv1mv1×100=100%

questions.q: A bullet of mass 200 g having initial kinetic energy 90 J is shot inside a long swimming pool as shown in the figure. If it's kinetic energy reduces to 40 J within 1 s, the minimum length of the pool, the bullet has to travel so that it completely comes to rest is
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let us assume that the motion of the bullet is of constant retardation inside the water.

Initial kinetic energy 12mv02=90 J

⇒v0=30 m s-1

Let the retardation is a, then after 1 s

12m30-a×12=40 J

⇒30-a=20

⇒a=10 m s-2

Stopping distance for the constant retardation is given by,

l=u22a=30220=45 m.

Therefore, the minimum length of the pool required is 45 m.

questions.q: The potential energy function (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></math> ) of a particle in a region of space is given as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>. Here <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>y</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>z</mi></math> are in meter. The magnitude of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> - component of force (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">N</mi></math> ) acting on the particle at point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given U=2x2+3y3+2z

The expression for the x-component of the force can be calculated as follows: 

Fx=-∂U∂x=-4x

Hence, at the point 1, 2, 3 m, the value of the force is given by

Fx=-4×1 N=4 N

questions.q: Potential energy as a function of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>U</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>10</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>B</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>5</mn></msup></mfrac></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> is the interatomic distance, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>B</mi></math> are positive constants. Given U=Ar10-Br5.

Now, for equilibrium, dUdr=0.

So, differentiating the given equation,

-10Ar11+5Br6=0

⇒10Ar11=5Br6⇒r5=2AB⇒r=2AB15

questions.q: A block of mass m, lying on a smooth horizontal surface, is attached to a spring (of negligible mass) of spring constant k. The other end of the spring is fixed, as shown in the figure. questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
When block attains maximum speed net force on m is zero. ∴F=kx

Or x=Fk

From work energy theorem

-12 k Fk2+FFk=12mVmax2

F22k=12mVmax2

questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the work done by a variable force is given by

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) to calculate the required work done.

W=∫04 (2+3x)dx=2x+32x204=[8+24] J=32 J

questions.q:
A block of mass 5 kg starting from rest pulled up on a smooth incline plane making an angle of 30° with horizontal with an effective acceleration of 1 m s-2. The power delivered by the puling force at t=10 s from the start is _____ W.
[Use g=10 m s-2]
(Calculate the nearest integer value)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let's consider the following free-body diagram:

From the above diagram, it can be written that

F-mgsin30°=ma   ...1

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) and solve to calculate the force applied on the block.

F-50 sin30°=5×1⇒F=5+25 N=30 N

The velocity of the block v at t=10 s can be written as

v=0+1 m s-2×10 s=10 m s-1

Hence, the required power is given by

P=Fv= 30 N×10 m s-1= 300 W

questions.q: A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> block moving at a speed of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>12</mn><msup><mrow><mo> </mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> compresses a spring through a distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>30</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> when its speed is halved. The spring constant of the spring will be _____ <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>Nm</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given: Mass of the block m=500 g, initial velocity of the block u=12 m s-1, and final velocity of the block v=u2=6 m s-1.

As non-conservative forces are not acting on the system we can conserve energy.

Thus, loss in kinetic energy of block = Gain in potential energy of spring

12mu2-12mv2=12kx2

12×0.5×122-12×0.5×62=12k×0.32

k=600 N m-1
